definition: Swarthy means having a dark complexion.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word swarthy. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know swarthy should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The opera's costume notes call for a swarthy pirate king, his dark complexion set off by a scarlet coat.
Fair names the lightest coloring on this scale, as far from swarthy as a complexion can be — the pale end of the ladder.
Tanned is darkness the sun lends and winter takes back; it stops short of swarthy, which names a complexion that is naturally deep-toned.

Dusky is a poet's word for soft, dark tones — dusky light, a dusky glow, a dusky complexion — describing shade in the moment rather than its source. Swarthy is strictly a complexion word: naturally dark skin, named in an older literary register. Dusk can fall on anything; swarthy fits only people.

Dark-complexioned is the plain, modern way to say someone has naturally dark coloring — the wording a passport office or a news report would choose. Swarthy means the same thing in an older, literary voice, at home in ballads and sea novels. The difference is register, not shade.

Sweart faded out of everyday English centuries ago — swart survives only in dialect and old poetry — so swarthy has no living relative to lean on. Its closest kin is across the border in German, where schwarz is still the ordinary word for 'black.'

In the memoir, the author's swarthy uncle stands out in every photograph of the pale northern village — olive-skinned and dark-haired, the one face the neighbors never mistook for anyone else's.
Swarthy is a literary, slightly old-fashioned word for having a dark complexion.
It describes coloring only — most often in ballads, novels, and old records — and says nothing about character; modern writing outside such contexts usually just says 'dark-skinned' or 'tanned.'
Swarthy belongs to ballads, sea novels, and old records — exactly where the SAT will show it to you.
It describes complexion only.
In your own writing, prefer 'dark-complexioned' or 'tanned'; reach for swarthy only when echoing that older literary voice.

Catalog entries had called him pale for two centuries -- an error of grime rather than of paint.
Cleaned, he is unmistakably swarthy: deep brown skin laid down in confident strokes, a complexion the painter observed from life, not a tan the sea lent him.
